title: Meier et al. (2016): Professor Question Preparation
instructions: State the conclusion first, then briefly explain the concept, selection and coding of 36 articles, article-level theme frequencies, stakeholder comparisons, and interpretive limits. Use the assigned source segment and preserve the distinction between reported themes and individual preferences.

cards.title: What does this review ask, and what does it conclude?
cards.answer_30s: The review compares definitions of a good death in 36 empirical studies representing patients, prebereaved or bereaved family members, and healthcare providers. Preferences for the dying process, pain-free status, and emotional well-being appeared most often overall, while the frequency of themes such as quality of life, dignity, and spirituality differed across perspectives. The authors call for individualized dialogue centered on the patient's viewpoint. These are patterns in the included literature, not a universal checklist of what every patient wants.

cards.title: How does a good death differ from the quality of death and dying?
cards.answer_30s: A good death concerns the multifaceted, individualized features considered desirable in the experience of dying. Quality of death and dying concerns the agreement between a person's preferences and other people's reports of how the person actually died. This review focuses on definitions explicitly offered from patient, family, and provider perspectives, rather than on an outcome score measuring that agreement. The authors also acknowledge criticism of imposing an external standard on an individual's dying experience.

cards.title: How did the search narrow 3,434 records to 36 articles?
cards.answer_30s: The database search identified 3,434 records. Title and abstract screening excluded 3,042, leaving 392 full texts for assessment. A further 356 were excluded, leaving 36 articles in the final analysis. The review required qualitative or quantitative evidence specifically defining or measuring a good death as a main aim or outcome. Related end-of-life topics were not automatically eligible simply because they concerned death or care.

cards.title: What designs and measures were represented?
cards.answer_30s: Of the 36 articles, 27 were qualitative, five quantitative, and four mixed-methods studies. Among the nine quantitative or mixed-methods articles, three used standardized good-death measures. The other six developed their own measures, including questionnaires with different numbers and kinds of items. This variation matters because the review combines findings produced through different approaches rather than results from a common instrument administered to one comparable population.

cards.title: How were the 11 core themes developed?
cards.answer_30s: Two researchers independently read all 36 articles using a grounded-theory-based process of coding consensus, co-occurrence, and comparison. Four consensus meetings helped establish the coding scheme, with a three-author meeting narrowing 38 initial themes to 11. Two researchers then independently mapped definitions to those themes. Reported interrater agreement was kappa .896, and remaining disagreements were resolved through discussion, consulting a third author when needed. I would report the kappa without reproducing the malformed p-value printed in the source.

cards.title: Why should the stakeholder-group counts not be added as distinct studies?
cards.answer_30s: Patient perspectives appeared in 20 articles, family perspectives in 10, and provider perspectives in 18. These categories overlap: 29 of the 36 articles were assigned to one group, two to two groups, and five to all three. The values 20, 10, and 18 are therefore the denominators for their respective perspective groups. Their sum is 48 group assignments, not 48 distinct studies or 48 participants.

cards.title: Why were no formal meta-analysis or study weights used?
cards.answer_30s: The studies differed in their methods and in the depth of demographic, diagnostic, treatment, and cognitive information, making formal statistical pooling inappropriate for these data. The authors also chose not to weight the combined qualitative and quantitative literature. They instead describe frequencies of the 11 themes within stakeholder sources. The reported percentages should be read as descriptive, unweighted theme frequencies, not precision-weighted pooled effect sizes or a direct estimate of individual preferences.

cards.title: What were the main characteristics of the included studies and patient samples?
cards.answer_30s: The studies were published from 1996 through 2015, and reported sample sizes ranged from three to 2,548, with a mean of 184.4. Patient ages ranged from 14 to 93. Half of the patient-perspective articles included people over 60; that does not mean half of all participants were over 60. Age reporting varied, with some studies giving only ranges, so I would avoid relying on the article's questionable pooled mean-age statement as a dependable summary of this heterogeneous population.

cards.title: What are the 11 core themes?
cards.answer_30s: They are preferences for the dying process, pain-free status, religiosity or spirituality, emotional well-being, life completion, treatment preferences, dignity, family, quality of life, relationships with healthcare providers, and other. Each contains two to four subthemes. Life completion, for example, includes saying goodbye, a sense of a life well lived, and acceptance of death. These are coding categories for the literature, not requirements that every individual must meet.

cards.title: Which three themes appeared most often overall, and what is the unit of those percentages?
cards.answer_30s: The Results section reports preferences for the dying process in 94% of articles, pain-free status in 81%, and emotional well-being in 64%. These percentages describe whether themes appeared in reports, not the percentage of all individual respondents endorsing them or their importance scores. The discussion's wording about pain-free status is inconsistent with the Results figure, so I would identify these specifically as the reported Results values and avoid presenting the discrepancy as resolved.

cards.title: Where did the three stakeholder perspectives converge most clearly?
cards.answer_30s: Preferences for the dying process appeared in 100% of patient-perspective articles, 100% of family-perspective articles, and 94% of provider-perspective articles. Pain-free status appeared in 85%, 90%, and 83%, respectively. Both themes were therefore frequent in every perspective group. The denominators are articles containing those perspectives, not individual patients, relatives, or providers, and high frequency does not establish identical personal priorities across those groups.

cards.title: What was the largest perspective difference, and how should it be interpreted?
cards.answer_30s: Quality of life appeared in 70% of family-perspective articles compared with 35% of patient-perspective articles. That is twice the article-level frequency, not proof that families value quality of life twice as much or understand patients better. Most family studies involved recollections after bereavement, and the authors suggest that families and patients may define quality of life differently. They call for further research rather than identifying one perspective as more accurate.

cards.title: Why does the dignity comparison not imply that patients value dignity less?
cards.answer_30s: Dignity appeared in 55% of patient-perspective articles and 70% of family-perspective articles. The authors caution that definitions vary, dignity may be represented within other themes, and patients may find it difficult to express the concept. They also cite other research on concerns about autonomy, respect, meaningful activity, and dignity. The comparison therefore cannot be read as a measure showing that dignity is less important to patients.

cards.title: How do the authors propose broadening care beyond physical symptoms?
cards.answer_30s: The review identifies emotional well-being as a recurring theme across patient, family, and provider perspectives. The authors argue for addressing psychological, social, and religious or spiritual concerns alongside pain and physical symptoms. They also call for more research on psychological assessment and appropriate interventions near the end of life. These are implications and research recommendations; the review does not establish that one fixed package meets every person's needs or evaluate the effectiveness of a specific intervention.

cards.title: What are the main methodological limitations?
cards.answer_30s: The review includes only English-language, peer-reviewed articles and combines studies with differing measures and uneven demographic, diagnostic, and other reporting. Timing between interviews and death was often unclear. Prebereavement family perspectives were poorly represented, and provider roles, end-of-life experience, and training were often combined or unspecified. The limited literature and some small descriptive differences also restricted statistical comparison. The reported patterns therefore should not be presented as statistically established population differences.

reading_response.title: Preparing a Reading Response
reading_response.instructions: Explain your impressions, methodological assessment, surprising findings, and family implications in your own words. Distinguish article-level theme frequencies from individual preferences and recommendations from demonstrated effects.

cards.title: Give a brief overall response to the review.
cards.answer_30s: I read the review as a reason for dialogue among people who may approach the same dying experience differently. Preferences for the dying process and pain-free status were commonly represented, but themes such as quality of life, dignity, and spirituality varied across the literature. For me, the central implication is to ask patients about their priorities and individualize care. The recurring themes offer a starting point for conversation, not a substitute for a particular patient's viewpoint.

cards.title: Which finding seemed most counterintuitive?
cards.answer_30s: I was struck that quality of life appeared in 70% of family-perspective articles but 35% of patient-perspective articles. I would not interpret that as families knowing the patient better or caring twice as much about quality of life. Most family studies were retrospective after bereavement, and the construct may have different meanings across groups. I see the descriptive difference as a reason to clarify preferences and meanings, while recognizing that the review does not directly test that proposed explanation.

cards.title: What was most interesting about the method?
cards.answer_30s: I appreciated the independent reading and explicit coding process used to make varied definitions comparable. Four consensus meetings helped develop the scheme, 38 initial themes were narrowed to 11, and independent coding yielded a reported kappa of .896. Disagreements were discussed with a third researcher when needed. This makes the construction of the categories visible, although strong coding agreement does not by itself establish the validity of every category or the representativeness of the underlying literature.

cards.title: Which finding did you read as common ground across perspectives?
cards.answer_30s: Preferences for the dying process and pain-free status were frequent across all three perspective groups. The former appeared in 100%, 100%, and 94% of patient, family, and provider articles; the latter in 85%, 90%, and 83%. These are article-level frequencies, not individual response rates. I would use them to begin a conversation about a person's priorities, while keeping room for themes that appeared less often. Lower frequency does not make a concern unimportant to a particular patient.

cards.title: Which analytic limitation matters most?
cards.answer_30s: I would emphasize the absence of formal meta-analysis and study weighting. Differences in reported patient characteristics, diagnoses, treatment, cognitive information, and methods limited what could be pooled, and the review combined qualitative and quantitative evidence. Its percentages are therefore a descriptive, unweighted summary of themes in the literature. I would not interpret them as precision-weighted effect estimates, population preference rates, or statistical tests of stakeholder differences.

cards.title: How would you connect the review to family research?
cards.answer_30s: Families are central to end-of-life care, but their views should not automatically stand in for the patient's preferences. I would investigate how patients, families, and providers discuss areas of agreement and difference, and whether addressing those themes changes patient-related outcomes. The authors call for earlier dialogue and better characterized, diverse samples. I see adapting care to the patient's values as a research and practice direction, not an intervention benefit already demonstrated by this review.
